newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia on currency watch as exports falter.
newsitem.headline: Asia on currency watch as exports falter.

text.p: Investors are keeping a close eye on Asia's generally strong currencies for any signs of depreciation to boost export competitiveness, analysts said.
A turnaround in Asian export growth was forecast by the first quarter of this year but while signs of recovery were increasing, most analysts said the immediate outlook was cloudy.
"The choice appears to be between slower growth and a weaker currency," SBC Warburg said in a recent report.

Many Asian currencies, linked directly or indirectly to the U.S. dollar, have been forced to appreciate in line with the dollar's spectacular 50-percent climb against the Japanese yen over the past two years.

The price of Asian exports has soared while overseas demand slumped, trapping many Asian economies in a vice that squeezed famously high economic growth rates and highlighted gaping current account deficits.
"(Exports) have made about as much progress as an asthmatic ant carrying some rather heavy shopping," SBC Warburg quipped.
Much of the speculation about currency depreciation started last month when analysts suddenly noticed a switch in foreign exchange policy by the Singaporean government.
The Singapore dollar, which until February enjoyed a long and steady appreciation against the U.S. dollar, suddenly started to falter, shedding three percent in the last two months.
"There is some evidence Singapore is considering some currency changes because of weakness in trade," said Jake van der Kamp, investment strategist at ABN Amro, Hoare Govett Asia.
The Singapore dollar has weakened to about 1.445 to the U.S. dollar from 1.3950 last December.
Investors are also keenly aware of Thailand's dilemma.
The Thai baht has dropped to 26 against the U.S. dollar from 25.40 last November, caught between weak exports and a heavily-indebted banking sector highly sensitive to interest rate adjustments.

"Singapore's behaviour raises the question of competitive devaluation in the region," SBC Warburg said. "Despite an outward appearance to the contrary, we suspect that Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines, to differing degrees, are watching developments in Thailand and Singapore closely."
But van der Kamp was not convinced it would happen. He argued that weaker currencies were not only an effective method of boosting exports, they invited inflation.
Overseas demand would dictate improvement in Asian exports, and there were concrete signs that demand was rising, he said.
Weakness in the Singapore dollar was rooted in a government policy objective to protect an exporting base and prevent the economy from becoming entirely dependent upon services.
"It is official government policy in Singapore to maintain an industrial base," he said. "They are scared that Kuala Lumpur and Jakarta would take back all the service trade."

Van der Kamp took comfort in improving trade figures across the region. Excluding China and India, he said the region's exports have grown one percent in U.S. dollar terms over the last six months from a decline of one percent last November.
That is still a long way from the 25 percent growth rates of early 1995, but enough of a turnaround to give hope.
"That's a six-month average, which is pretty long term, so if you've got a turn on that you know you're really up," he said.
